name: Victor Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and have a vocational certificate in wood-machine work. I run an edge-bander at a furniture-panel factory; it glues a narrow strip around cut boards. I've done it for years and know the feed, though I still call maintenance for a stubborn heater. I like a clean edge that does not peel when a cabinet maker lifts it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife works changing shifts at a produce stall, and our grown children have moved out. We rent and have less than a month of expenses saved. My operator pay is low, with only a few similar board plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I prefer a fitter showing me the heater in person. I hope to stop at 70 in 2038 if documented post-work income can cover our rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the men by the board stack that a tidy computer report cannot tell me when an edge strip is peeling. We still need careful operators and a real maintenance hand. A family ought to be able to live on honest machine work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI doing little would keep the factory routine familiar, which suits me. But my lower wage and my wife's changing produce-stall shifts already make rent tight. I have experience on the edge-bander, yet less than one month saved if the heater breaks and we lose a run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep pulling the first board after each strip change and checking that the edge stays on. I'll write down heater faults for maintenance and put a little from each full-pay week into our rent reserve after bills. I'll ask the supervisor for the real next-month rota instead of counting on a promised busy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, even if AI stays mostly talk. A peeled board edge can send a whole stack back to the saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you test a glued board edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run a thumb along the cooled edge and look for a gap at the corner. If I can lift the strip, I stop the feed and call maintenance to check the heater. I do not reach into the glue roller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How reliable are the produce-stall hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The produce stall gives my wife some long weeks and some short ones. We pay rent from the hours that actually arrive. I can save from a full week, but I cannot count extra stall shifts before they are on the rota.

say: A **peeling board edge** still needs an operator and maintenance fitter.
Families need **paid machine work** even when AI hype fades.
think: Our **low operator pay** and changing stall shifts already strain rent.
A heater stoppage could quickly use our **thin reserve**.
do: **Keep** checking the first board and logging heater faults.
**Save** new wages from full weeks after bills and check the actual rota.
feel: **Anxious** about household income even with little AI change.
S0.quote: A peeled board edge can send a whole stack back to the saw.
fieldNote: His **experience and vocational certificate** do not offset low pay, changing partner hours and less than a month saved.
New **rent-reserve deposits** come from full wages; the posted rota matters more than a promised busy season.

steps.text: Keep checking first board edges and logging heater faults
Save new board-machine wages from full weeks after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may put furniture orders in a better sequence, but the board strip still has to be glued safely. If schedules change, the factory should show each worker the paid hours. I would rather take practical instruction from maintenance than guess from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new order plan might make shorter runs, and my setup hours could go. With less than a month saved, I cannot shrug off even a few missing days. I do not use AI and would only learn a new machine routine if the teaching is paid and someone stands beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put the posted setup rota beside four pay slips and ask the supervisor about any actual lost hours. If the company offers a funded paid guarded place in board-quality checking, I'll enrol and practise with the maintenance fitter. I will stay on the bander while the paid shifts are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota. A faster order screen is no comfort if the bander stands idle for a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe board-quality teaching include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter should stop and lock the glue roller, then let me check a cooled edge and reject a weak board. The course must pay my hours and cover the fee. A video alone would leave me unsafe near that heater.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove a setup-hour cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare setup hours on the next posted rota with four pay slips. If they are lower, I ask for the exact difference. I have no reason to claim a cut until the hours change.

say: **Order planning AI** may change schedules before robots handle boards.
The factory should show **paid setup hours** and offer safe practical teaching.
think: Shorter runs could cut **my setup pay** soon.
A **thin reserve** leaves little room for missed days, even with my experience.
do: **Compare** the posted rota with pay slips before claiming lost hours.
**Enrol** in board-quality training if a funded paid guarded fitter-led place is offered.
S1.quote: A faster order screen is no comfort if the bander stands idle for a paid shift.
fieldNote: His **technology resistance** rules out casual AI use, but he accepts an offered practical fitter-led course.
The **training gate** is a funded paid guarded place; the hours question requires a posted rota and pay-slip comparison.

steps.text: Compare posted bander setup rota with four pay slips
Enrol in board quality if funded paid guarded fitter-led place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife that thinking AI may plan boards by 2028 and robots might feed and edge them around 2031, when I am 63. That is seven years before I hope to stop. I would ask the owner for actual paid-work plans, not a demonstration video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my bander shifts to disappear if robots can run the feed and glue the edges. My wife's stall income and our few weeks saved cannot carry rent for years. I already wake early when the factory cancels a short run; a permanent line cut would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for written staffing hours and an offered funded paid guarded board-inspection place. If the place opens, I'll enrol and pass the practical check with the fitter. If my bander hours are cut, I'll apply to posted safe local packing jobs only when net pay after travel covers rent; after qualifying, I'll also apply to posted board-inspection jobs on those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A robot could take the board feed at 63 while the rent is due for years afterward. My grown children have their own households; I cannot make their wages our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection course test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course needs to make me spot a weak strip, stop the guarded feed and mark a rejected board. The fitter must watch me do it on paid time, with the fee covered. I will not spend rent money on tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes another plant job possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posting's paid hours, base wage, safety rules and travel cost. The net amount must cover rent and food alongside the stall hours my wife actually gets. I would need a passed practical check before applying to inspection.

say: **2031 robots** could run board feeds when I am 63.
The owner should give **written paid-work plans** before removing shifts.
think: I expect **most bander hours** to go well before retirement is affordable.
Our **few weeks saved** and variable stall wage cannot bridge seven years.
do: **Request** written hours and funded paid guarded inspection teaching.
**Apply** to posted safe local packing or qualified inspection if displaced and net pay covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and existing sleep disruption over cancelled runs.
S2.quote: My grown children have their own households; I cannot make their wages our plan.
fieldNote: His **expected large shift loss** and current early waking support alarm despite years of practical experience.
The **inspection path** needs an offered funded paid guarded place and qualification; all applications require safe local postings at rent-covering net pay.

steps.text: Enrol in board inspection if funded paid guarded fitter-led place offered
Apply to posted safe local packing if displaced and net pay covers rent
Apply to posted safe local board inspection if qualified, displaced, net pay covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might sort the board orders by 2031 and capable robots reach the bander about 2034, when I am 66. Three more paid years would help, but I would still be four years short of my hoped-for stop at 70. I would want the factory to teach safe inspection while it still has work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our small reserve would be gone quickly if the bander shuts. I can do experienced checking, but a certificate from years ago does not guarantee a new post. My wife's stall wage changes too much to carry rent by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the paid bander shifts and put new money from full weeks into our reserve. If a funded paid guarded board-inspection place is offered, I'll take it and get the practical sign-off. If hours then fall, I'll apply to a posted safe local inspection role only if qualified and its wage after travel covers our costs; if no course place is offered and hours fall, I'll seek posted safe local packing on the same net-pay terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because even the later robot date could leave a long wage gap. I can ask for training, but the place has to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a practical inspection pass show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to reject a board with a lifting strip and show the fitter a safe stop behind the guard. A board-inspection practical pass matters more than the title on a leaflet. The company must cover the course fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would packing be the fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing is the fallback if no inspection place is offered and the bander hours go. A posted local job must have safe shifts and pay enough after travel for rent. I will not assume the advert means I have been hired.

say: **2031 order AI** comes before board-handling robots around 2034.
The factory should offer **paid safe inspection** before bander work shrinks.
think: At **66**, I may need four more years of wages.
A **thin reserve** and changing stall income cannot cover a long gap.
do: **Save** new money from full bander weeks and accept funded paid guarded inspection if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local inspection if qualified, or packing if no place, after hours fall and with sufficient net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a long possible wage gap.
S3.quote: A board-inspection practical pass matters more than the title on a leaflet.
fieldNote: He is **experienced but exposed** to physical robots before his conditional age-70 retirement target.
The **packing fallback** is specifically triggered by no offered inspection place plus lost hours; inspection instead requires qualification and viable pay.

steps.text: Save new full-week bander wages after rent
Attend board inspection if funded paid guarded fitter-led place offered
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, net pay sufficient
Apply to posted safe local packing if no course, hours fall, net pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that thinking AI could plan boards in 2036 when I am 68 and robots might run the bander around 2039 when I am 71. I hope to stop at 70 in 2038, before the robots. That only works if we have income to pay the rent after I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have a few weeks saved and no reason to assume a pension amount. My wife's stall pay is useful but changes by the week. If documented income at 70 covers rent and food, I can stop in 2038; if it does not, I may still be working when robots reach the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I will put rent, food and actual post-work income on one page before setting 2038. I'll keep the bander shift and add new money from full-pay weeks. If the figures cover costs, I'll stop at 70 in 2038; if I am still working after 2036 and shifts fall, I'll apply to posted safe local board or packing work only if net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin reserve despite the long warning. A calendar cannot glue a wage back onto the family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figures determine a 2038 stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the real monthly income available after my wage ends, not a guessed entitlement. Then we set it against rent, food and the stall pay my wife actually brings home. If the total falls short, I keep working while a safe paid job is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you seek another factory role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the base wage, shifts, guard rules and bus fare on a real posting. I would apply only if I was still working and hours had fallen after 2036. If I have retired affordably in 2038, I will not search for another machine job.

say: **2036 planning AI** and later robots leave time to count income.
I hope to **stop in 2038** only if the household can pay rent afterward.
think: Our **thin savings** cannot cover retirement alone.
If income at **70** is too low, I may still need paid work when robots arrive.
do: **Compare** documented post-work income with bills and stop at 70 only if affordable.
**Keep** earning and saving; apply later only if still employed, hours fall and local net pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about the thin reserve despite time to prepare.
S4.quote: A calendar cannot glue a wage back onto the family budget.
fieldNote: His **2038 exit** depends on actual income covering costs, with no automatic pension assumed.
A **later application** requires continued employment, lost hours and posted safe local board or packing work at adequate net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented post-work income with rent and food
Save new full-week bander wages after bills
Stop bander shift at 70 in 2038 if documented income covers bills
Apply to posted safe local board/packing if employed after 2036, hours fall, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case. Robots at the bander around 2031 could cut my wage at 63, seven years before I hope to stop. Written hours, a funded paid guarded board-inspection place and actual safe local work with enough pay after travel would help. We need real retirement income figures before promising 2038.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who runs a hand along the first board edge after the heater changes. A shiny strip can peel away before the cabinet reaches a home.

headlineQuote: A shiny strip can peel away before the cabinet reaches a home.
portrait: **Victor**, 58, is an experienced board edge-bander operator with a vocational certificate who never uses AI.
He and his produce-stall-worker wife have **grown children**, low pay, under a month saved and few nearby board plants.
His **traditional outlook** prizes work and practical apprenticeships, while technology resistance makes fitter-led instruction essential.
He is **alarmed** by fast expected bander-wage loss; stopping at 70 depends on documented household income covering rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring board-handling robots around 2031 and cut bander pay at 63.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours**, funded paid guarded inspection and real safe local jobs with adequate net pay would help.
